results.title: Tools For Open Reproducible Science | Earth Data Science - Earth Lab
results.content: * Describe how `bash`, `git`, `GitHub` and `Jupyter` can help you implement open reproducible science workflows. To implement open science workflows, you need tools that help you document, automate, and share your work. Throughout this textbook, you will learn how to use open science tools that will help you:. While there are many tools that support open reproducible science, this textbook uses: `bash`, `git`,`GitHub.com`, and `Python` in `Jupyter Notebooks`. Scientific programming using an open source, free programming language like `R` or `Python`, is an effective and efficient way to begin building a workflow that is both reproducible and that can be easily shared. Later in this textbook, you will learn how to use a `Bash` (a specific implementation of `Shell`) to access and manage files on your computer and to run other programs that can be started or run from the `Terminal`, such as `Jupyter Notebook` and `git`. Later in this textbook, you will learn how to use the `git`/`GitHub` workflow to implement version control for your files, share work and collaborate with others. The Jupyter project is an open source effort that evolved from the IPython project to support interactive data science and computing. JupyterLab is flexible: you can configure and arrange the user interface to support a wide range of workflows in data science, scientific computing, and machine learning. Connecting your entire workflow including accessing the data, processing methods and outputs is an important part of open reproducible science. `Jupyter Notebook` files can help you connect your workflow by allowing you to write and run code interactively as well as organize your code with documentation and results within individual `Jupyter Notebook` files. As described previously, `Python` is a widely used programming language in the sciences and provides strong functionality for working with a variety of data types and formats. Writing and organizing your `Python` code within `Jupyter Notebook` files supports open reproducible science through documentation of data inputs, code for analysis and visualization, and results – all within one file that can be easily shared with others. In later chapters, you will learn how to use `Jupyter Notebook` to write and run `Python` code for analysis and visualization of earth and environmental science data.

This one-hour tutorial introduces new users to version 5 of PyMC, a powerful Python, open source library for probabilistic programming and Bayesian statistical modeling. Participants will learn the fundamentals of PyMC, best practices for installation and setup, and gain hands-on experience building their first Bayesian model. WinBUGS and OpenBUGS provided invaluable experience in Bayesian modeling for beginners, and paved the way for the development of PyMC as well as other tools that made it easier to implement Bayesian inference methods. In 2003, Chris Fonnesbeck began writing the first version of PyMC, with the goal of being able to build Bayesian models in Python. PyMC 1.0 was released in 2005. Learn more about the history of PyMC up to 2023 here: PyMC: Past, Present, and Future — PyMC project website. PyMC has experienced an estimated 40-60% adoption growth since 2022, establishing itself as the most accessible entry point for Python developers into probabilistic programming through its intuitive syntax and seamless integration with the PyData ecosystem. While Stan remains the academic gold standard and NumPyro excels in raw computational performance, PyMC’s recent JAX integration now delivers competitive speed while maintaining the familiar, Pythonic workflow that makes Bayesian modeling approachable for newcomers. * Optional: watch the video on the history of PyMC: PyMC: Past, Present, and Future — PyMC project website. * pymc.io: Home — PyMC project website. **Introduction to PyMC and Probabilistic Programming****. * What is PyMC and its role in the Python data science ecosystem. * Understanding PyMC’s computational backends. * Understanding PyMC’s relationship with ArviZ. **The PyMC Ecosystem and Resources****. * Related packages (Bambi, PyMC-experimental). * Finding and using PyMC example notebooks. * How AI/LLMs are changing PyMC workflows. ## post by reshamas on Aug 12, 2025. ## post by reshamas on Aug 15, 2025.
